title: Sell Mineral Rights in Texas
group: Permian, Eagle Ford, Haynesville TX, Barnett, Anadarko TX
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Texas | Permian, Eagle Ford & More
metaDescription: Texas mineral owner in the Permian, Eagle Ford, or Barnett? Each region has its own decline curve and value pattern. See how to read yours before you sell.
heroLead: Texas isn't one oil state, it's five or six different ones stacked under a single set of state lines, and where your minerals sit matters more than the fact that you own Texas minerals at all.
intro: No state spans as much variety in oil and gas geology as Texas. West Texas holds the Permian basin, the most actively drilled oil play in the country, split into the Midland basin on the east side and the Delaware basin to the west. South Texas has the Eagle Ford, an oil and condensate window that's matured considerably since its boom years. North Texas carries the Barnett, mostly a gas play now well into its long decline tail. Northeast Texas touches the Haynesville, another gas-heavy formation. And the Texas Panhandle sits on the western edge of the Anadarko basin, with older conventional production alongside newer activity.

Because these plays are so different in age, product mix, and current activity level, a fair offer on your interest starts with figuring out which of these regions, and honestly which specific county, your minerals actually sit in.

sections.heading: Permian basin: the state's most active oil region
paragraphs: Midland, Ector, Reeves, and Loving counties, along with dozens of others across West Texas, sit inside the Permian, where operators continue stacking horizontal wells across multiple formations including the Wolfcamp, Spraberry, and Bone Spring. A lot of Permian acreage still has real drilling upside left, which a buyer factors into an offer alongside your well's current production.

Wells here follow the familiar shale pattern: a strong first year or two, a steep decline, then a longer shallower tail. Where your specific well sits on that curve, combined with whether your unit still has undrilled locations, does more to set your value than the Permian's reputation as a whole.

sections.heading: Eagle Ford: a maturing oil and condensate play
paragraphs: The Eagle Ford across counties like Karnes, DeWitt, and La Salle saw its heaviest drilling roughly a decade or more ago, which means a large share of Eagle Ford wells are now further along their decline curve, producing steadier but smaller volumes than during the boom years.

That maturity isn't a downside by itself. It simply means an Eagle Ford offer is priced more around demonstrated tail production and less around speculative future drilling compared to a fresher Permian unit.

sections.heading: Barnett and Haynesville: mostly gas, not oil
paragraphs: If your Texas interest sits in the Barnett, around Tarrant, Denton, or Johnson County, or the Haynesville in the northeast corner of the state, you're most likely holding a gas royalty rather than an oil one. Both plays have been producing for well over a decade, and much of that production is now on a long, mature decline tail with limited new drilling.
Value here tracks natural gas markets rather than crude oil, which move on different cycles, so don't assume your Barnett or Haynesville check should follow oil price headlines.

sections.heading: Texas Panhandle: layered conventional and newer plays
paragraphs: The Panhandle's Anadarko basin acreage carries decades of conventional oil and gas production layered under some newer horizontal activity. Older vertical wells in this region are typically well into a stable, low-volume tail, while newer wells behave more like other modern shale development with a steeper early decline.

Because both types of wells coexist in the same counties, checking your specific well's spud date and recent production history matters even more here than in the more uniformly-aged Permian or Eagle Ford.

sections.heading: Texas ownership realities across regions
paragraphs: Texas mineral title is often split across generations of ranch and farm families, particularly in West and South Texas, where large historic land grants have divided into dozens of small fractional interests over a century. Courthouse records vary widely in how well they're organized county to county, from Midland's active recorder's office to smaller rural counties with thinner staff.

If your title is unclear, shared among heirs, or tied to an old estate that was never fully probated, talk to your attorney or a title examiner before signing any conveyance, particularly on active Permian or Eagle Ford acreage where accurate legal description matters for pricing correctly.

faqs.question: How do I know which Texas play my minerals are in?
faqs.answer: Start with the county. West Texas counties like Midland, Reeves, and Loving are Permian. South Texas counties like Karnes and DeWitt are Eagle Ford. North Texas is Barnett, and the Panhandle is Anadarko basin.

faqs.question: Why would Permian basin minerals be worth more than similar Barnett minerals?
faqs.answer: Permian wells are more often oil-focused with active ongoing drilling and remaining reserves, while Barnett wells are largely mature gas production with limited new-well upside, which typically prices lower.

faqs.question: Is Eagle Ford production still valuable if the boom years are over?
faqs.answer: Yes, mature Eagle Ford wells still produce steady oil and condensate volumes. The value reflects that steadier tail production rather than boom-era output, and pricing varies with the specific well's recent history.

faqs.question: Does Texas have different rules for mineral rights sales by region?
faqs.answer: The legal process is the same statewide, but title complexity, drilling activity, and product mix vary significantly by region, which is why an offer should be based on your specific well and county, not a statewide average.

faqs.question: What if my Texas interest is in an area I've never heard of?
faqs.answer: Texas has oil and gas activity in dozens of counties beyond the well-known plays. Your division order or a title examiner can confirm the formation and current operator regardless of how well-known the area is.
